fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. Zedekiah says, “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.” (Jeremiah 38:5). A king handing the whole thing over is something to see. I think the officials didn't need to be told twice.

That would be a king taking charge, friend, but that's not what he says. Zedekiah answers, “He is in your hands, since the king can do nothing to stop you.” (Jeremiah 38:5). The officials get the green light. He's handing Jeremiah over, not holding on to him.

Sand is a fair guess for a dry pit, friend, but the text says something else. The cistern, a pit for storing water, “…had no water but only mud, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud.” (Jeremiah 38:6). Mud is the word the Bible uses. This is a heavy part of the story.

It's true, friend, and the text says it plainly. Ebed-melech, a court official from Cush, tells the king, “…these men have acted wickedly in all that they have done to Jeremiah the prophet.” (Jeremiah 38:9). He goes out from the king's palace and says it to the king. Not everybody in that palace was going along with it.

That's the reason, baker. Ebed-melech says Jeremiah will starve “…for there is no more bread in the city.” (Jeremiah 38:9). Down in the mud, I think that sounds dire. Jeremiah's own words had mentioned famine too (Jeremiah 38:2).

Not this time, baker. The king commands Ebed-melech, “Take thirty men from here with you and pull Jeremiah the prophet out of the cistern before he dies.” (Jeremiah 38:10). That's a yes. Zedekiah says to pull him out.

I see how you got there, since Jeremiah sank into the mud. But the text says something else. Ebed-melech calls, “Put these worn-out rags and clothes under your arms to pad the ropes.” (Jeremiah 38:12). Cleaning up could wait. Getting out came first.
That's an easy fear to picture after the mud, friend. But Jeremiah says something else: “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). Death is the word he uses, not the pit.

Babylon is a good guess in this chapter, but it isn't what Jeremiah says here. He tells King Zedekiah, “If I tell you, you will surely put me to death.” (Jeremiah 38:15). Nothing about a trip. The word is death.

That's a reasonable guess, friend, but it isn't the promise. Zedekiah swears, “…I will not kill you, nor will I deliver you into the hands of these men who are seeking your life.” (Jeremiah 38:16). It's about not killing him and not handing him over. Sending him out of the city isn't part of it.

Yes, baker. If Zedekiah surrenders, Jeremiah says, “…you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.” (Jeremiah 38:17). The word comes from the LORD God of Hosts, the God of Israel. It comes with an if: if he surrenders to the officers of the king of Babylon.

Close in feel, friend, but not the word. The LORD says through Jeremiah, “…you will live, this city will not be burned down, and you and your household will survive.” (Jeremiah 38:17). The word the LORD uses is burned. Emptying isn't mentioned.

You got it, baker. Zedekiah says, “I am afraid of the Jews who have deserted to the Chaldeans, for the Chaldeans may deliver me into their hands to abuse me.” (Jeremiah 38:19). I think that fear is real to him. He says it right after Jeremiah tells him what surrender would mean.

That's the word, baker. Jeremiah says that if the king refuses to surrender, the women who remain in the palace will say, “…Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.” (Jeremiah 38:22). Those are the king's own trusted friends. I think that line would sting.

That would be a happier ending, friend, but the text has the opposite. Jeremiah says that if the king refuses to surrender, the women will say, “…Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.” (Jeremiah 38:22). Those trusted friends are the ones who left him.

A warning would be something, baker, but that's not the word. Jeremiah says that if the king refuses to surrender, the women will say, “…Your feet sank into the mire, and they deserted you.” (Jeremiah 38:22). The friends he trusted are the ones who deserted him.

Yes, baker. Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to say, “I was presenting to the king my petition that he not return me to the house of Jonathan to die there.” (Jeremiah 38:26). That's the line Jeremiah is given for the officials. It's a handy one.

That's it, baker. They said no more to him, “…for no one had overheard the conversation.” (Jeremiah 38:27). Jeremiah gave them the exact words the king had commanded him to say. Nobody overheard the conversation, and that's the reason the text gives.

Yes, baker. “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.” (Jeremiah 38:28). It's what the LORD's word said would happen to the city. Hard to read, but the story isn't over.

Rebuilding is a hopeful word, friend, but it's not this one. The text says, “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.” (Jeremiah 38:28). It ends with the city taken. A hard word to land on, but the story isn't over.

I wish that were it, baker, but the text says the opposite. “And Jeremiah remained in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured.” (Jeremiah 38:28). That's what Jeremiah had said the LORD's word would bring. A heavy way to end this stop, but the story isn't over.
